title: This Tiny Idaho Town Is Getting Super-Powered New Reactors — And They Fit on a Truck!
summary: Have you ever seen a nuclear reactor on the back of a truck? In Atomic City, Idaho — a tiny town with just 52 people — that’s exactly what’s happening. At a bar where the regulars order drinks called “atomic bombs,” locals aren’t scared of nuclear energy. “I live 10 miles away, and I’m fine,” says bar owner Vickie O’Haro. “I’m not glowing in the dark, you know?” Nearby, at a huge 900-square-mile lab (that’s almost as big as Rhode Island!), a company called Deployable Energy just made its test reactor go “critical.” That means it had a steady chain reaction for the first time — a huge step toward making electricity. But this isn’t like the giant nuclear plants you might picture. These are micro reactors, small enough to fit on a truck and power about 1,000 homes instead of a million. “It’s something deployable,” says the company’s leader, Maul. “It is a fundamentally different proposition.” The idea is to mass-produce them and send them to remote towns, military bases, or even data centers that need lots of power. President Trump has sped up approvals for these projects. But not everyone is cheering. Some scientists worry that safety rules are being cut too fast. Edwin Lyman from the Union of Concerned Scientists says he has “no confidence” in the government’s oversight. Plus, the commission that checks nuclear safety has lost many experts. Still, in Atomic City, people are excited. O’Haro thinks it’s “pretty cool” to see this happen in her backyard. Would you want a micro reactor in your neighborhood?
why_it_matters: Micro reactors could one day power your school or neighborhood without big power plants, but they also raise important questions about safety that might affect your community.

background_read: Nuclear reactors have been used for over 60 years to make electricity — the first ones were built in the 1950s and were huge.
Idaho is home to the Idaho National Laboratory, one of the largest nuclear research sites in the world, where many new reactor designs are tested.
President Trump, who took office again in 2025, has supported building new types of nuclear energy, including small reactors that can be built faster than big power plants.
